intro: A decade of making, mostly because I wanted to know what would happen.

scraps.title: Before Github.
scraps.descriptor: Websites, tools, unfinished games
popover: When I was twelve, a friend showed me my name scrolling across a browser using the `<marquee>` tag. It amazed me that I could make the browser show whatever I wanted.

School and entrance-exam prep took up most of my time, but I spent whatever was left making things with friends: websites, painting tools, and games. We always imagined someone using them. Mostly, nobody did.
Somewhere along the way, my school selected me as one of ten students for a trip to Singapore. I’m still grateful for that. My friends still ask, “What school does that?” Hahaha.

scraps.title: Voice-controlled chess
scraps.descriptor: Say a move. Board responds.
popover: A Python course ended with tic-tac-toe and blackjack. I wanted something with enough logic that I couldn't hold the whole thing in my head at once. Chess seemed like a good idea. Then I decided I should be able to say a move out loud and watch the board respond.
It became the first thing I ever pushed to GitHub. I still play occasionally, around 2000 on Lichess.

scraps.title: 8×8 LED matrix hex generator
scraps.descriptor: Draw pixels, get Arduino hex
popover: Someone from the electronics department had the hardware and was missing a small piece of software. I told him I could make it in a day. And I did.
We swapped rooms the next semester.
Seven years later, we started Faradworks together.

scraps.title: WitnessHarmony
scraps.descriptor: Turn songs into game levels
popover: I wanted a game whose levels came from the music itself. So I pulled beats out of a song, turned them into timestamps and packaged the whole thing as a Windows executable.
Then I wrote a nine-step manual explaining how to use it.
That manual may be the earliest thing I still have where I was clearly imagining a stranger trying to use what I made.

scraps.title: Koch islands
scraps.descriptor: Grow shapes from simple rules
popover: Exploring bio-inspired simulation.
Just rewriting rules, a little turtle walking them, and strange, beautiful islands appearing on the screen.

scraps.title: Agents crossing a 2D map
scraps.descriptor: Tiles that hurt, slow, or block
popover: I had seen Atari games being played by a single agent and wanted to try it myself. So: tiles that behaved differently. Fire took health, ice took time, mountains blocked the way entirely.

I got as far as a 4×4 map and a table of state values. The agent found a short route to the goal, but didn’t care enough about walking through fire. Getting somewhere quickly and getting there safely were two different things to teach it.

scraps.title: Personal Genie
scraps.descriptor: A few questions to find your next gadget
popover: Could a few questions capture someone's preferences as a vector, then match it against TVs, phones and laptops? That was the idea behind Personal Genie. I later learned about content-based and collaborative filtering. Turns out I had wandered into recommender systems.
Built for a hackathon at SRM, which meant flying to Chennai for the final round. We finished in the top ten.

scraps.title: Mentify
scraps.descriptor: Mental health chatbot
popover: Built a mental-health app over a weekend at HackCBS hackathon, with activities, an analysis screen and a chatbot. I was learning Flutter because mobile dev was hot back then.
We spent the night sitting in corridors. That turned out to be my last overnight hackathon.

scraps.title: TensorRT Swish plugin
scraps.descriptor: Custom C++ plugin, ~3× faster LeNet-5 inference
popover: An NVIDIA bootcamp gave us 45 days to build a native TensorRT plugin. My teammate and I spent half of them solving the wrong problem, until a session with NVIDIA engineers cleared things up. I must have read the developer guide fifteen times. We wrote a Swish plugin in C++ and measured roughly 3× faster inference on LeNet-5.
We came first. There were two teams.

scraps.title: DeepConnect
scraps.descriptor: You teach, you learn
popover: I love teaching. At the end of 2019, LeadingIndia.AI appointed me to mentor four winter interns on food recognition. We worked with Mask R-CNN, with sessions on convolutions and loss functions along the way. Two months later, they presented their work to an evaluation panel.

We launched DeepConnect in the second half of 2020, the same semester I was a teaching assistant. The motto was 'you teach, you learn'. We ran teaching sessions and put the videos on YouTube. Then internships took us in different directions.
In 2022, I tutored Python for a few months. One client was in Singapore, so some sessions meant getting up at 3 a.m.

scraps.title: Face recognition for attendance
scraps.descriptor: Three projects, three Python frameworks
popover: Face recognition kept finding its way back to me. In 2019, I built a Flask app with a teammate while barely knowing Flask or databases. In 2022, I fixed a client's Django API. In 2024, I built and deployed a secured FastAPI service for a client.
Somehow, that added up to three Python web frameworks and three face-recognition libraries. None of it was planned.

scraps.title: BEL detection and tracking
scraps.descriptor: Restricted-area surveillance with RGB and infrared
popover: A project from Bharat Electronics Limited through Bennett University, under Dr. Vipul Kumar Mishra. We tried YOLOv4 and YOLOv5 for detection, with DeepSORT for tracking, using RGB footage by day and infrared by night. Training eventually moved to a remote DGX system after we couldn't get GPU quota on Google Cloud.

Our detector could spot someone partly hidden behind cover and miss someone standing right in front of it. We revised the dataset several times, varying backgrounds and lighting, until it handled both.

scraps.title: Skill Sight
scraps.descriptor: What next to learn, and who else is learning it
popover: Bennett was paying for everyone's Coursera courses, so we built a way to see what friends were learning and find someone taking the same course to build something with. We also gathered campus tech events scattered across WhatsApp groups into one place.
We launched at skillsight.in (the domain belongs to somebody else now), university email addresses only, with course tracks, progress and chat.
We never figured out how to keep the course catalogue updated across different platforms, or why a student would pay for it.

scraps.title: CTR optimization
scraps.descriptor: Choosing ad audiences from past campaign logs
popover: A project for Times Internet under Dr. Gaurav Singhal's guidance: could we choose better audiences for ads using only past campaign logs? We used counterfactual bandits to learn a targeting policy, estimating what a different choice might have earned.

Of 6.8 million rows, only 6,696 recorded ads actually being shown. With so little usable data, we generated combinations from those rows to create 343,000 trajectories. The reward model fit the training data well but failed on the held-out month. It seemed to be learning our generated combinations rather than anything that carried over to real data.

scraps.title: Crop radiation prediction
scraps.descriptor: Net radiation, from solar radiation and canopy temperature
popover: Under the guidance of Dr. Gaurav Singhal, I built the training pipeline: regression splines, gradient boosting and a small neural network, all driven by one config file.
The work was published in the International Journal of Biometeorology. My first peer-reviewed paper.

scraps.title: Industrial PPE detection
scraps.descriptor: Detecting missing safety gear (helmets, vests, gloves, glasses) in camera feeds
popover: At Datakalp, I worked on PPE detection under Dr. Kalpit Desai's guidance. Helmet data was available. For safety vests, gloves and glasses, we ended up hunting through Getty Images and other sites.
Different sites had different safety rules, so the pipeline had to support different combinations of PPE checks. I worked through data collection, modelling and GStreamer pipelines to get it running.

scraps.title: Video annotation tool
scraps.descriptor: Marking the nine steps of handwashing
popover: I spent about fifteen to twenty days building a web-based video annotation tool at Datakalp. The team used it to mark the nine steps of handwashing in footage.

scraps.title: Dealer EOS map
scraps.descriptor: Dealer response times and performance, mapped across India
popover: At VECV, I built an interactive map showing dealer performance across India, including how often they reached breakdowns on time within their zones. It went out monthly to the head office and regional centres.
I built the mapping interface using Folium with custom Leaflet plugins for specialized markers, since the standard map markers didn't support what we needed.

scraps.title: Vehicle application analytics
scraps.descriptor: Analysing truck behaviour and costs on specific routes
popover: At VECV, I combined CAN logs from BS4 and BS6 trucks with gearbox tables and chassis records to analyse driving patterns, fuel consumption and mileage on specific routes. I built a Streamlit app around it, which sales teams used in customer presentations and Product Development used to understand vehicle behaviour.

scraps.title: Job-card analyser
scraps.descriptor: Checking vehicle alerts against workshop findings
popover: At VECV, we needed to check whether vehicle alerts matched what technicians actually found in the workshop. I built an NLP pipeline to compare workshop notes with alerts, bringing the analysis down from 3–5 days to about ten minutes.

scraps.title: Tri-colour palette
scraps.descriptor: One colour in, five out
popover: I was choosing colours for data visualizations and built a little tool to help.

scraps.title: Bagmodels
scraps.descriptor: A Python library for ranking documents against a query
popover: A small library of bag-of-words retrieval algorithms. I wrote my own Python implementation and put it on PyPI as bagmodels. I checked recently and was surprised it was still getting downloads four years later.

scraps.title: Speech to emotion
scraps.descriptor: An animated face that reacts to your voice
popover: I trained a speech classifier on RAVDESS to recognise eight emotions, then connected it to an animated face. It updates every half-second as you speak.

scraps.title: WonderMirror
scraps.descriptor: 3D virtual try-on
popover: I never liked trying on clothes. My teammate and I worked on a way to try them on a 3D version of yourself instead, using body reconstruction and virtual garment fitting.
It was our final-year project, but I thought there was a company in it. I skipped campus placements because I wanted to build my own thing.
We eventually stopped. The garment-fitting methods we needed were still at the research stage, and most of the useful 3D datasets we found were proprietary.

scraps.title: Keystroke anomaly detection
scraps.descriptor: Can typing patterns reveal an intruder?
popover: A client wanted to know whether typing patterns could reveal that someone else was using an account. I explored it using reinforcement learning.

scraps.title: Optimus
scraps.descriptor: Planning a pharma plant
popover: Demand, inventory, recipes, blending, machines, changeovers, constraints, schedules, planners.
The planner I was trying to automate turned out to belong inside the system.

scraps.title: TaxTalk
scraps.descriptor: A tax answer machine, running locally
popover: A question-answering bot for tax, running a quantised Mistral-7B on my own machine against a knowledge base I kept updating.
I built the landing page too, with pricing and sign-up, before there was anything to sign up for.

scraps.title: GSTN analytics hackathon
scraps.descriptor: Predict the target, no domain knowledge
popover: A government hackathon: predict a binary target with no domain knowledge about what any of the columns meant.
Average precision 0.94, ROC-AUC 0.995, and a written report in the repo.

scraps.title: Kaggle: problematic internet use
scraps.descriptor: Child Mind Institute competition
popover: A Kaggle competition on problematic internet use in children.
The repo carries more than the submission. The notes in it record where cross-validation and the leaderboard disagreed, which turned out to be the interesting part.

scraps.title: Cataract classifier
scraps.descriptor: Eye photo in, answer out, behind an API
popover: A fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 that decides whether an eye shows a cataract, at 98.36% on the holdout set.
This is where I stopped shipping notebooks. It has a FastAPI backend, a Streamlit front end and a written report.

scraps.title: Trajectory evaluation
scraps.descriptor: Reading the path, not the answer
popover: At Turing I was producing coding and reasoning data, comparing models against each other, and reading back what agents had actually done.
Somewhere in there the final answer started to matter less to me than the path the model took to get there.

scraps.title: ssnet
scraps.descriptor: Chagas from a twelve-lead ECG
popover: PhysioNet's 2025 challenge asked whether Chagas disease could be predicted from a twelve-lead ECG. I wrote the data preparation for three separate source corpora and two transformer architectures with sparsity-aware attention.
I never made a final submission. The README says archived.

scraps.title: Kanban calendar
scraps.descriptor: Built without reading the code
popover: A desktop planner that puts a kanban board over a time-block calendar, so a card can be constrained to the block it belongs in. Electron and React, and everything stays on the machine.
I did not read a single line of it. It is the first thing I built entirely by asking for it.
I do not use it any more.

scraps.title: Cars24 vs Spinny
scraps.descriptor: Six listings, ranked by price to condition
popover: A multi-agent pipeline that pulls specs and condition signals out of used-car listings, then ranks them by price against condition.

One agent reads the disclosed facts. Another looks at the photographs and judges the panels, the cabin, the tyres, the engine bay. The composite leans seventy percent towards the facts, because the photographs are interpretation.
The weighting only shifts towards the photographs as the evaluation covers more ground.
